lesson.title: Continuity: Making 'No Breaks in the Curve' Precise
lesson.summary: A function is continuous where its graph can be traced without lifting the pencil, and turning that intuition into a limit-based test lets us check the property exactly instead of just eyeballing it.
lesson.body:
The intuitive starting point for continuity is familiar: a function is continuous on some interval if its graph has no holes, jumps, or breaks there, the kind of curve you could trace from end to end without ever lifting your pen. That picture is a useful mental image, but it is not precise enough to check algebraically for a specific complicated function, which is exactly why continuity leans on the limit and limit existence ideas already built up: continuity is defined in terms of limits, not simply judged by how a curve looks.

The working definition is this: a function f is continuous at x = a when the limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists, meaning the left-hand and right-hand limits both exist and agree, and that limit equals the actual function value f(a). In plain language, continuity says the value the function approaches near a and the value it actually lands on at a are one and the same number, no surprises. This three-part idea, defined, limit exists, and the two match, is unpacked in full detail as a checkable test in the next two chapters.

There are three basic ways continuity can fail, and each corresponds to a different kind of limit trouble already seen in earlier chapters. A removable discontinuity, a hole, happens when the limit exists but either does not match f(a) or f(a) is missing entirely, exactly like (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) at x = 3 from the limits-from-tables chapter, where the limit is 6 but the original formula is undefined there. A jump discontinuity happens when the left-hand and right-hand limits both exist individually but disagree with each other, so the two-sided limit fails to exist at all, as in the step-function example from limits-from-graphs. An infinite discontinuity happens when the function has a vertical asymptote and the limit is infinite rather than any finite number, as with 1/x^2 near x = 0 from the infinite-limit chapter.

Worked example of a continuous function: f(x) = 3x^2 - 5x + 1 is continuous at every real number. Direct substitution always works here, lim as x approaches a of f(x) equals f(a) for every single value of a, with no algebra required to see it, because a polynomial is built from nothing more than sums and products of continuous building blocks, namely constants and x itself, and sums and products of continuous functions remain continuous, a fact that follows from the limit laws.

Worked example of a discontinuous function: f(x) = 1/(x - 2) is continuous at every real number except x = 2, where it is undefined and has an infinite discontinuity, a vertical asymptote. Everywhere else it behaves perfectly: at x = 5, for instance, f(5) = 1/3, and lim as x approaches 5 of f(x) also equals 1/3, matching exactly, so continuity holds at every point of this function's domain except that one troublesome value.

Because continuity is such a well-behaved, useful property, continuous functions can be evaluated by direct substitution, composed safely as in limit-of-composition, and underpin many later calculus results, the next two chapters zoom in on how to test continuity rigorously at one specific point, using an explicit three-condition checklist rather than a general picture.
